cheeseburger-on-wheat-bun-1-small-patty.title: Cheeseburger on wheat bun, 1 small patty

content.title: About
content.content: A cheeseburger on a wheat bun with one small beef patty (1669) is a classic fast‑food item that combines melted cheese, a grilled patty, fresh vegetables and sauce between a soft wheat bun.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cheeseburger was served in the United States in the 1920s.
A wheat bun gives a lighter texture compared with the traditional brioche bun.
A small patty usually weighs about 45 g, making the sandwich less calorie‑dense than a standard cheeseburger.
American processed cheese is often used because it melts quickly.
Cheeseburgers are commonly served with fries and a drink as a popular "combo".

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium, which supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese are rich in B12, B6 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: The beef patty is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed.

items.title: Fiber from the bun
items.content: The wheat bun provides a modest amount of dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High calories and saturated fat
items.content: Cheeseburgers can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces and cheese add sodium, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Gluten in the bun
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheeseburgers are typically eaten by hand, often split in half to keep the filling together. Adding fresh vegetables such as tomato, lettuce, and onion, or swapping to a lighter sauce, can reduce calories if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared cheeseburger in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. Reheat in an oven or grill to keep the bun crisp and the cheese melted.

cookie-peanut-butter-with-rice-cereal-no.title: Cookie, Peanut Butter with Rice Cereal, No Bake

content.title: About
content.content: A ready‑to‑eat snack that combines peanut butter, rice cereal and a touch of sweetener into a no‑bake cookie. It is shelf‑stable, quick to prepare and popular among sweet‑tooth and fitness enthusiasts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cookie requires no heat – ingredients are simply mixed and shaped.
Rice cereal gives a light, crunchy texture and makes the product airy.
Peanut butter provides plant‑based protein and healthy fats.
Often used as a post‑workout snack for fast energy.
Several flavor variations exist – classic, chocolate‑drizzled, and with dried fruit.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter supplies about 25 % protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats in peanut butter promote heart health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Rice cereal adds fiber that aids normal digestion.

items.title: Moderate sugar content
items.content: The recipe uses a modest amount of sugar, making it more suitable for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Combined carbs from the cereal and fats from the peanut butter provide rapid and sustained energy.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: The product can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to peanuts.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of its fat and sugar content, portions should be moderated.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions contain added salt; those monitoring sodium should choose a low‑salt option.

items.title: Potential gluten
items.content: If processed with gluten‑containing additives, it may not be suitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy straight from the pack, crumble into yogurt or smoothies, or use as a base for homemade energy bars. For a firmer bite, briefly microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a cool, dry place in a sealed container. For storage longer than three months, refrigerate to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: The chocolate croissant is a French pastry consisting of a buttery, flaky dough rolled into a crescent shape and filled with dark chocolate. Its crisp outer layer and melt‑in‑your‑mouth interior make it a popular breakfast item and snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Croissants originated in Austria in the 17th century and were later refined by French bakers.
In France the chocolate version is called “pain au chocolat.”
Traditional fillings use dark chocolate with at least 70 % cocoa content.
The flaky texture comes from repeatedly folding butter into the dough, creating over 100 layers after baking.
In some countries the pastry is dusted with powdered sugar or chopped nuts before serving.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the dough and fats from butter and chocolate provides a quick energy boost.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Rich in magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in chocolate supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Cocoa contributes iron, which helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Mood enhancer
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which can improve mood.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Chocolate croissants are calorie‑dense; moderation is important for weight management.

items.title: Sugar and saturated fat
items.content: The amount of sugar and butter can negatively affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Cocoa allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chocolate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate croissants are best enjoyed warm, straight from the oven. Eat them as a snack, pair with coffee, milk, or fruit yogurt. For a lighter taste, lightly dust with powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store croissants in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage keep them refrigerated (up to 5 days) or frozen (up to 1 month). Reheat in the oven for 5‑7 minutes before serving to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg salad with Italian dressing is a classic American dish from the early 1960s. Core ingredients are hard‑boiled eggs, mayonnaise, mustard and a fragrant Italian dressing made from olive oil, vinegar, oregano, basil and garlic. Served cold as a snack or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish first appeared in the United States in the early 1960s as Italian cuisine gained popularity.
The Italian dressing gives the salad a distinctive herbaceous flavor compared to the plain mayo‑only egg salad.
It is often used as a filling for sandwiches and baguettes.
Modern recipes sometimes add chopped pickles or celery for extra crunch.
The 1961 recipe was featured in magazines such as Better Homes and Gardens and Cook’s Illustrated.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil in the dressing supplies monounsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs are rich in B2, B6 and B12, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Herbs (oregano, basil) and garlic contain polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Eggs and olive oil provide modest amounts of vitamin D and calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked eggs may harbor salmonella; always use fully cooked eggs.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Mayonnaise and olive oil make the dish high in calories, so watch portion sizes.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People with egg allergy can experience mild to severe reactions.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; those with high blood cholesterol should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled as a dip, in salad bowls, or on crackers. It also works well as a sandwich filling, on toast, or as a side to vegetable dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing.

content.title: About
content.content: Meatless spinach quiche is a baked tart made with a pastry crust, eggs, cream, and fresh spinach, prepared without any meat. It offers a creamy flavor, the fresh aroma of spinach, and a lightly crisp crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach quiche originates from French cuisine, where quiche is traditionally filled with a variety of ingredients.
It is often served as a vegetarian appetizer for breakfast, lunch, or a light dinner.
The crust can be shortcrust or puff pastry, depending on personal preference.
Spinach retains most of its nutrients when briefly cooked.
The meatless version makes the dish suitable for vegetarians and those avoiding red meat.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Spinach provides iron, essential for blood formation and maintaining energy levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in spinach help protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Thanks to the high vegetable content, the meatless quiche is moderately caloric while being filling.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Eggs and cheese in the filling supply a complete animal‑derived protein.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: The quiche contains eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cream and cheese can increase sodium levels; monitor added salt.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach is high in oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in predisposed persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the quiche warm or at room temperature, cut into portions. It pairs well with a fresh salad, tomato sauce, or a light yogurt dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked quiche in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to 180 °C to restore crust crispness if desired.

summer-squash-yellow-or-green-frozen-coo.title: Summer squash, yellow or green, frozen, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (zucchini) is an annual plant of the Cucurbitaceae family grown for its edible fruits. The frozen product consists of pre‑sliced yellow or green pieces that are flash‑frozen to retain most of their flavor and nutrients. When cooked with a little oil they become tender and aromatic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the same family as pumpkin, melon and watermelon.
Yellow varieties get their color from the natural pigment xanthophyll.
Freezing is done within 30–45 minutes after harvest, minimizing vitamin loss.
A quick sauté in a small amount of oil keeps the squash slightly crisp.
In many cuisines it is used in stews, soups and casseroles.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Provides beta‑carotene (vitamin A)
items.content: Beta‑carotene is important for vision and skin health.

items.title: Cucurbit allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to summer squash.

items.title: Sodium content in processed product
items.content: If the frozen squash is salted, consider the total sodium intake in the diet.

items.title: Possible pesticide residues
items.content: When buying frozen vegetables, choose reputable brands that test for residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté the frozen squash pieces in a skillet with a little oil for 5–7 minutes until tender and lightly golden. Add them to pasta, rice, omelets, soups, or serve as a side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen squash in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 1–2 days and do not refreeze.
